nodes.subject: Unicomp Model M owner discussion
nodes.object: One owner reports an 11-year survivor, while other participants report failure after about 18 months, a probable logic-board failure after about six years, and switch wear after roughly 12 years.

support_spans.exact_quote: It's served me well so far and shows no sign of slowing down.
Funny, my Unicomp from the same era died after about 18 months. They refused any support after the 12 month warranty.
Mine broke after about 6 years, i probably just needed a new logic board but not having nkey rollover was a nightmare for gaming so i just recycled it.
I finally managed to wear out the switches on mine after coding with it for 12 years or so.

nodes.subject: Sun68 owner report
nodes.object: A hot-swap PCB failed after a few months, troubleshooting did not revive it, no replacement was found, and the owner recommends buying a backup PCB.

support_spans.exact_quote: The hotswap PCB I bought with the keyboard has officially crapped out on me after a few months of use. I worked with the manufacturers (who were responsive and helpful) to flash, reset, and otherwise troubleshoot the PCB. No dice. Unfortunately, the PCB is gone and I am in the unenviable position of having a lovely keyboard that doesn't work.
I've checked all vendor websites, ebay, discord, reddit, etc. no luck so far.
If you entering the group buy market, and your wallet can afford the additional expense, I would recommend always picking up a back-up PCB as part of the groupbuy.

nodes.subject: Keyboard technology article
nodes.object: Gold contacts can limit oxidation, keyboard processors debounce contacts, and hot-swap sockets permit switch replacement without the typical direct solder connection.

support_spans.exact_quote: Many switch designs use gold for contact material to prolong the lifetime of the switch  by preventing switch failure from oxidization.
Hot-swappable keyboards are keyboards in which switches can be pulled out and replaced without requiring the typical solder connection.
Instead of the switch pins being directly soldered to the keyboard's PCB , hot-swap sockets are instead soldered on.
To resolve this, the processor in a keyboard debounces the keystrokes, by averaging the signal over time to produce one "confirmed" keystroke that (usually) corresponds to a single press or release.

nodes.subject: Keycap article
nodes.object: Keycaps are sold in replacement sets, PBT is harder and long-wearing, and doubleshot legends do not fade even as a keycap wears.

support_spans.exact_quote: Keycaps can be bought in replacement sets for a keyboard.
PBT is a harder long-wearing material with a "sandier" feel and should not yellow as much as ABS over time.
This means that there is no chance of the legend ever fading or getting removed, even as the keycap wears down.

nodes.subject: Sun68 owner report
nodes.object: A hot-swap Sun68 PCB failed after a few months despite troubleshooting, leaving the keyboard unusable when no replacement PCB could be found. The owner recommends buying a backup PCB, showing that switch hot-swap does not cover controller or PCB failure and that spare availability is part of serviceability.

accepted_phrases: A Sun68 owner reports a failed hot-swap PCB after a few months, unsuccessful troubleshooting, and no available replacement, illustrating why hot-swappable switches do not make the whole board repairable without PCB spares.

support_spans.exact_quote: The hotswap PCB I bought with the keyboard has officially crapped out on me after a few months of use. I worked with the manufacturers (who were responsive and helpful) to flash, reset, and otherwise troubleshoot the PCB. No dice. Unfortunately, the PCB is gone and I am in the unenviable position of having a lovely keyboard that doesn't work.

nodes.subject: keyboard switch and hot-swap mechanisms
nodes.object: Metal contacts can be protected against oxidation, processors debounce contact oscillation, and hot-swap sockets let switches be replaced without normal soldering. These generic mechanisms describe switch and socket boundaries; they do not establish a complete keyboard's lifetime or make its PCB replaceable.

accepted_phrases: Keyboard mechanisms explain metal-contact oxidation protection, debounce, and switch replacement through hot-swap sockets, but none of those generic facts proves whole-board longevity or PCB serviceability.

support_spans.exact_quote: Many switch designs use gold for contact material to prolong the lifetime of the switch  by preventing switch failure from oxidization.
Hot-swappable keyboards are keyboards in which switches can be pulled out and replaced without requiring the typical solder connection.
Instead of the switch pins being directly soldered to the keyboard's PCB , hot-swap sockets are instead soldered on.
To resolve this, the processor in a keyboard debounces the keystrokes, by averaging the signal over time to produce one "confirmed" keystroke that (usually) corresponds to a single press or release.

nodes.subject: keycap wear and replacement
nodes.object: Keycaps are replaceable wear items, PBT is described as harder and long-wearing, and doubleshot legends cannot fade or be removed even as the keycap wears. These facts can reduce legend-wear risk but do not establish switch, cable, socket, controller, or PCB longevity.

accepted_phrases: Keycaps can be replaced; PBT is harder and long-wearing; and doubleshot legends do not fade even as caps wear, so legend wear is separable from whole-board failure.

support_spans.exact_quote: Keycaps can be bought in replacement sets for a keyboard.
PBT is a harder long-wearing material with a "sandier" feel and should not yellow as much as ABS over time.
This means that there is no chance of the legend ever fading or getting removed, even as the keycap wears down.

nodes.subject: current keyboard durability matrix
nodes.object: The Punkston is the cheapest and has the strongest displayed aggregate among the three, but only seller-level switch-cycle and keycap claims. The CODE V3 adds a detachable cable and a similar 50-million-cycle switch claim at the highest price without captured hot-swap wording. The RK100 has the lowest aggregate but the broadest stated replacement path through MX-compatible hot swapping, four spare switches, PBT keycaps, and an included cable.

nodes.subject: switch-cycle claim and whole-board lifetime
nodes.object: Seller claims about 50-million-cycle switches are physically plausible component claims, but generic mechanisms and the Sun68 PCB failure show that sockets, controller or PCB, cable, and other components remain independent failure paths. A switch number cannot be promoted to a ten-year complete-keyboard guarantee.

nodes.subject: long-use owner evidence
nodes.object: The snapshot contains individual 11-year Unicomp, almost-four-year NYM96, and approximately 15-year-old secondhand Logitech G15 observations. The Unicomp thread also includes failures and support complaints at very different ages. Together they show that long service is possible and that outcomes vary, but they do not yield a model failure rate or prove any current shopping listing will last a decade.

nodes.subject: keycap shine and legend durability
nodes.object: Visible shine on the four-year NYM96 is compatible with continued board use. Replacement sets, PBT wear properties, and doubleshot legends separate cosmetic or legend wear from electronics failure. Product keycap claims therefore affect a replaceable wear item and cannot establish complete-board lifespan.

nodes.subject: replaceable failure points and spare availability
nodes.object: RK100 seller wording covers switch replacement and includes spares; CODE V3 wording covers cable replacement; keycaps are generally replaceable. None of those paths covers a failed controller or PCB. The Sun68 report makes PCB availability a gating repairability question, so warranty, replacement PCB supply, and other spares must be verified separately.

nodes.subject: evidence-bounded decade keyboard choice
nodes.object: No captured current listing is a proven decade winner. Choose the RK100 only as the repairability-first current-shopping fallback, not as a BIFL guarantee; treat Unicomp as the strongest but mixed longitudinal reference rather than a captured catalog option; and require confirmation of warranty, replacement PCB, cable, switch, and keycap availability before purchase.
